questions.q: In textile studies, what is a 'fiber'?
options: A large piece of woven cloth used for making suits.
The basic, hair-like unit of raw material used in making yarns and fabrics.
The mechanical part of a sewing machine.
A special chemical used to wash clothes.
questions.explain: A fiber is the smallest visible unit of any textile product; it is a fine, thread-like strand that is spun into yarn, which is then woven or knitted into fabric.

questions.q: During the weaving process of producing textiles, the lengthwise threads that run straight on the loom are called:
options: Weft
Warp
Selvedge
Bias
questions.explain: In weaving, the warp threads are the stationary, lengthwise threads held in tension on a frame or loom, through which the transverse weft threads are drawn.

questions.q: The crosswise yarns that are woven in and out of the warp yarns to create a fabric are called:
options: Selvedge
Bias
Warp
Weft
questions.explain: The weft (or filling) is the thread or yarn that is drawn through and inserted over-and-under the warp yarns to form the woven fabric.

questions.q: Textile fibers are generally divided into natural and synthetic (man-made) fibers. Which of the following is a natural fiber derived from an animal source?
options: Cotton
Silk
Nylon
Linen
questions.explain: Silk is a natural protein fiber produced by the silkworm, which is an animal. Cotton and linen are natural plant fibers, and nylon is synthetic.

questions.q: Which of the following represents a synthetic (man-made) fiber?
options: Polyester
Wool
Cotton
Silk
questions.explain: Polyester is a synthetic fiber, meaning it is artificially manufactured from chemical polymers rather than harvested from plants or animals.

questions.q: Which property makes cotton fabrics highly suitable for wearing in hot weather climates?
options: It shrinks significantly in cold water.
It conducts heat well and is highly absorbent of body sweat.
It builds up extreme static electricity.
It melts when exposed to sunlight.
questions.explain: Cotton is very absorbent and a good conductor of heat, meaning it pulls heat and sweat away from the body, keeping the wearer cool in hot weather.

questions.q: Why is it important to study the properties of different textiles in Home Economics?
options: To ensure fabrics are destroyed correctly.
To know which fibers should be fed to domestic animals.
To guide consumers in making the right choices for specific uses and knowing how to properly care for them.
To avoid buying clothes entirely.
questions.explain: Studying textiles helps individuals understand how fabrics behave, ensuring they choose the appropriate fabric for a task (e.g., upholstery vs. underwear) and use the right laundry methods.

questions.q: When laundering natural wool fabrics, which of the following practices should be strictly avoided to prevent the garment from shrinking or felting?
options: Washing it by hand gently
Using warm or very hot water and scrubbing vigorously
Drying it flat on a clean surface
Using a mild detergent
questions.explain: Wool fibers have scales that interlock when exposed to heat, moisture, and agitation. Washing in hot water with rough scrubbing causes the wool to irreversibly shrink and felt.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key difference between natural and synthetic fibers?
options: Natural fibers melt when exposed to fire, while synthetic fibers burn to ash.
Synthetic fibers are highly absorbent, while natural fibers repel water.
Natural fibers come from plants and animals, while synthetic fibers are produced from chemicals.
Synthetic fibers can only be dyed in dark colors, while natural fibers cannot be dyed.
questions.explain: Natural fibers are derived from natural sources like plants (cotton, linen) and animals (silk, wool). Synthetic fibers are man-made from chemical polymers (nylon, polyester).

questions.q: In the production of simple textiles, such as a woven table mat, which local material is commonly used as the weaving yarn?
options: Raffia or palm fronds
Solid metal wire
Broken glass threads
Ceramic strips
questions.explain: Raffia, dried grass, and palm fronds are easily accessible local materials often used in schools to teach the basic principles of weaving mats and baskets.

questions.q: Which property makes linen suitable for making heavy-duty household items like tablecloths and strong upholstery?
options: It melts easily when washed in warm water.
It is extremely weak and tears quickly.
It is stronger than cotton and becomes even stronger when wet.
It stretches continuously and never holds its shape.
questions.explain: Linen, made from the flax plant, is highly valued for its exceptional strength and durability, which actually increases when the fabric is wet, making it great for household linen.

questions.q: When ironing a garment made entirely of synthetic fibers like nylon or polyester, what ironing temperature should generally be used?
options: The maximum hot setting on the iron.
A low or cool iron setting.
Ironing should only be done with boiling water.
Synthetic fibers cannot be ironed under any circumstance.
questions.explain: Synthetic fibers are thermoplastic, meaning they can easily scorch or melt under high heat. Therefore, they should be ironed using a low or cool heat setting.

questions.q: What does the term 'yarn' refer to in textile production?
options: The finished dress worn on the body.
A long, continuous length of interlocked fibers used for sewing, weaving, or knitting.
The wooden frame used to hold threads tightly.
A liquid dye used to add color to fabrics.
questions.explain: Yarn is produced by spinning raw fibers together into a long, continuous strand, which is then used to construct fabrics through weaving, knitting, or crocheting.
